ozet: With two ships' separate cargo holds in Knowledge Harbor, Piko explains why virtual environments are needed, the venv commands, and sharing a package list.

giris.anlatim: Day 23: Virtual environments! In this lesson you'll learn why virtual environments matter, the venv commands, and how to share your package list.

cikis.anlatim: The interactive version of this lesson is waiting for you at 30gunde.com.tr. Write your code right in the browser, run it instantly, and finish the tasks!
maddeler: Write and run code in your browser
Learn Python step by step in 30 days

sahneler.anlatim: Hi, I'm Piko! Two ships sit side by side at Knowledge Harbor: one carries fish, the other carries flowers. Imagine if the cargo got mixed up! Each ship has its own hold. Python projects should have their own hold too. It's called a virtual environment.

Let's see the problem. Your game project needs pygame 2.5, and an old project needs 2.1. If the computer has only one box of packages, both can't be installed at once; update one and the other breaks. A virtual environment gives each project its own box.

maddeler: One box: one of them breaks
Virtual environment: a box for each project

sahneler.anlatim: These commands are typed into the terminal while you're in the project folder. The first sets up an environment called dot venv. Then you activate it: activate in the Scripts folder on Windows, or the source command on macOS and Linux. To close it, deactivate is enough.
If you see .venv in parentheses at the start of the terminal line, the environment is open. Now every package you install with pip install goes only into this project.

maddeler: pip install pygame → only for this project

sahneler.anlatim: A common mistake: installing a package in one environment and running the program in another, or forgetting to activate the environment. Python can't find the package and gives a ModuleNotFoundError. Open the environment first, then run it.

The environment folder is big and isn't shared. Instead, we share the package list: pip freeze writes the list into a requirements file. Your friend sets up their own environment and installs the same packages. The .venv folder also goes into gitignore.
There's a similar trap in code. I assigned the list to the site variable and added flask to site. What do you think happens to the game list?

ekran.kod:
game = ["pygame"]
site = game
site.append("flask")
print("Game:", game)

sahneler.anlatim: Game changed too! Because both names point to the same box. Just like two projects sharing a single box of packages.

ekran.kod:
game = ["pygame"]
site = game
site.append("flask")
print("Game:", game)

sahneler.anlatim: The fix is to take a separate copy. With copy, site gets its own box, and game stays as it was. A virtual environment does exactly this for projects.

ekran.kod:
game = ["pygame"]
site = game.copy()
site.append("flask")
print("Game:", game)
print("Site:", site)

sahneler.anlatim: Let's imitate environments with a dictionary. Different versions of the same package live in two projects without ever getting mixed up.
In the tasks you'll produce the environment commands, take a separate copy of a list, and find version clashes between two projects. In the project you're choosing which files to share.
In short: set up a virtual environment for each project, activate it, install packages inside it, and share only the list.

maddeler: Virtual environment = a package box just for the project

sahneler.anlatim: The holds are spotless, well done! Tomorrow we stop by the harbor's records office. We'll make numbers talk with the mean, the median and NumPy arrays. See you!
